How to choose braiding hair

Your braider will tell you what to bring. These basics help you buy the right hair first time.

  • Ask how many packs. Pack sizes differ a lot between brands, so always ask your braider how many packs of which hair the style needs.
  • Pre-stretched or regular. Pre-stretched hair has tapered ends, so it is quicker to braid and gives a neater finish. Regular hair needs stretching by hand first.
  • Know the colour codes. 1 is jet black, 1B is off black, 2 is dark brown, 4 is medium brown, 27 is honey blonde, 30 is auburn and 613 is light blonde. A code starting with T, such as T1B/30, is a two-tone or ombre colour.

Curl types and porosity

Two things that help you pick products that suit your hair.

  • Type 2, wavy. Loose S-shaped waves that can go flat or frizzy. Light products work best.
  • Type 3, curly. Springy curls and ringlets. Define them on damp hair with a cream or gel.
  • Type 4, coily. Tight coils and zig-zags that dry out fastest. Add moisture, then seal it in with oil or butter.
  • Porosity. This is how easily your hair takes in and holds water. If water beads on your hair and products sit on top, it is likely low porosity, so use lighter products and a little warmth. If it soaks up water fast and dries fast, it is likely high porosity, so use richer creams and seal with oil.
  • Most people have more than one curl type on their head.

  • 1. Detangle first. Work in sections with your fingers or a wide-tooth comb, starting at the ends.

  • 5. Leave-in and seal. Apply a leave-in to damp hair, then a little oil or butter to hold the moisture.
  • 6. Style gently. Twists, braids or a bun keep hair stretched and protected until next wash day.

Starting and caring for locs

What to know before you book a loctician.

  • Ways to start. Common starter methods are comb coils, two-strand twists, braids and interlocking. Sisterlocks are a trademarked small-loc method fitted by trained consultants.
  • Be patient. Locs take months to mature, and they go through a frizzy stage on the way.
  • Retwist on schedule. Your loctician will tell you how often. Many people go every four to eight weeks. Too often, or too tight, can thin the roots.
  • Wash and dry properly. Clean locs lock better. Rinse shampoo out fully and let locs dry all the way through.
  • Keep products light. Heavy waxes and creams can leave build-up inside the loc.

Protecting your edges

Tight styles can damage the hairline over time. Here is how to avoid it.

  • Speak up if it hurts. Braids, ponytails and weaves should not be painful. Ask your stylist to loosen anything that pulls.
  • Know the warning signs. Soreness, small bumps or a hairline that looks thinner mean the style is too tight.
  • Take breaks. Give your hair a rest between braided or sewn-in styles.
  • Use a little edge control. A small amount is enough. Wash it out regularly so it does not build up.
  • Cover at night. A satin scarf protects your edges while you sleep.
  • If you notice hair loss that does not grow back, speak to your GP or a trichologist.
